mainEntity.name: My site is a shop and it is a bit slow. Is that not normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Being a shop is not a reason for slowness. The basket and the gateway do have some inherent work, but the home page and product pages should not be slow. If they are, the cause is usually heavy photos, weak hosting or an extra plugin, and all three can be fixed.

mainEntity.name: How small should a product photo be?

acceptedAnswer.text: As small as the size it is displayed at on the site. A several megabyte phone photo is unnecessary for a page that shows the image a few hundred pixels wide; a compressed version of the same photo, at the sharpness the eye actually sees, is several times lighter. Make it a habit before uploading any photo.

mainEntity.name: I bought cheap hosting. Is it really the culprit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes yes and sometimes no. First check the photos and plugins, which are in your own hands. If those are fine and the site is still slow at busy hours, the hosting cannot answer for your shop, and changing it is more effective than any other optimization.

mainEntity.name: Should I fix speed first or the site’s look first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Speed first. The customer has to see the page before its look can do anything. The good news is that lightening a site is usually cheaper and faster than a redesign, and after it, any design works better on a fast site.

Site speed
Why website speed matters for sales, and what makes your site slow

A customer taps your site’s link from Instagram and the page stays white. A few seconds later they are back where they were: they never saw the price, never saw the product. Website speed is the customer’s first meeting with your shop, and very often their last.
25 November 2026·7 min read·The dadmor team

In this article

  1. The mobile customer does not wait
  2. What makes a shop site slow?
  3. Measure your site’s speed yourself
  4. The right order to fix slowness: photos first
  5. What counts as fast enough?
  6. In short

Summary

  1. Most of your customers arrive on a phone, on mobile data. A page that opens late has lost the customer before the product was even seen.
  2. The most common cause of slowness is your own heavy photos; after that, cheap crowded hosting, and themes and plugins piled on top of each other. Most of it is cheap to fix.
  3. Measure the speed with your own phone first, then fix in order of impact: photos, extra plugins, hosting. A redesign is the last step, not the first.

In a physical shop, a customer who stands in front of a closed door walks to the shop next door. Online, that door is a page that is still loading. The difference is that here you do not even see how many came and turned back; sales just drop, and nobody knows why.

Website speed means the time between the customer tapping your link and being able to see the product and press the buy button. That time should be measured on a phone and on the customer’s ordinary mobile data, not on your office Wi-Fi and your own laptop, where everything is fast.
In this article we say what makes a shop site slow, how to measure its speed yourself, and in what order to fix it so your money is spent where it matters most first.
The mobile customer does not wait

Your customer arrives from your DMs and your bio link, on a phone, in the middle of the day, on mobile data. For them, your site is one of several pages they open today. If the home page and the product page take long to open, they go back and buy from another page or site that opened sooner. It is not your product or your price; they never got that far.

The important point is that slowness usually shows itself in the worst place: the product page and checkout. The customer has come all the way to the till and is kept waiting there. In Traffic but no sales we list the places a customer is lost between arriving and buying; speed is the first of them, and the only one where the customer never even entered the shop.
What makes a shop site slow?

items: Heavy photos: the most common cause. A photo taken on a phone is several megabytes, and for a product page it needs to be a fraction of that. Ten products with raw photos means a page that effectively never opens on mobile data.

Cheap, crowded hosting: a host that packs hundreds of sites onto one weak server answers everyone late at busy hours. For a shop that actually sells, the cheapest hosting is usually the most expensive choice.

Themes and plugins piled up: every plugin installed one day for a small job and left behind costs something on every visit. Sites that have collected plugins for years have slowed under their own weight.
Video and large files on the home page: an autoplaying video, extra fonts and scripts turn the home page, which should be the lightest page, into the heaviest page of the site.

blocks.html: Measure your site’s speed yourself

items: On your own phone, with Wi-Fi off and mobile data on, open your site and count how long it takes until you can see a product. This is the simplest and most honest test, and it is exactly what the customer experiences.
Use free speed testing tools and test the home page and one product page separately; the product page number matters more, because buying starts there.
Repeat the test once at a busy hour of the day; weak hosting shows itself exactly then, not at midnight when you happen to test.

blocks.html: The right order to fix slowness: photos first

items: Lighten the photos: shrink and compress every product photo to the size it is actually shown at on the site. This single job makes the biggest change in most shops and costs nothing.
Remove extra plugins: any plugin whose job you do not know, or whose job something else has taken over, should go. In speed, less is faster.
Change the hosting: if the server cannot answer, no optimization saves it. Choose hosting fit for a shop by its real resources, not only by its price.
Turn on caching and compression: one time technical jobs that can be enabled on most sites so pages reach the customer lighter and readier.

blocks.html: Do not reverse this order. A full redesign of a site whose problem is heavy photos and weak hosting spends a lot of money and brings the same slowness back with a fresh look.
Speed cannot be compensated for with pretty design; a customer who never saw the page likes no design at all. Opening first, beauty second.
What counts as fast enough?

There is no magic number, and do not trust anyone who gives you an exact, guaranteed one. The practical measure is this: the home page and the product page, on an ordinary phone and ordinary mobile data, open without an annoying pause, and the customer can scroll and press the buy button right away. If you got bored during your own test, the customer feels exactly the same.

Speed is not a one time job either. Every new product with a heavy photo and every new plugin can slow it down again. Repeat the same phone test once a month to catch new slowness early. On our website building page we explain that we count speed as part of the build from day one, not a repair done at the end.
In short

Website speed is respect for the customer’s time, and you see its effect directly in sales, because a customer who stays finally gets the chance to buy. Start by measuring with your own phone and fix in order: photos, plugins, hosting. Most shops do not need a redesign to become fast; they need to become lighter.
Your site is slow and you do not know where it comes from?

Measure it with the phone test first; half the answer shows up right there. If you want your new site built fast from day one, the project estimator shows its cost and time, and the website building page shows how we treat speed from the start.
Frequently asked questions

My site is a shop and it is a bit slow. Is that not normal?

Being a shop is not a reason for slowness. The basket and the gateway do have some inherent work, but the home page and product pages should not be slow. If they are, the cause is usually heavy photos, weak hosting or an extra plugin, and all three can be fixed.

How small should a product photo be?

As small as the size it is displayed at on the site. A several megabyte phone photo is unnecessary for a page that shows the image a few hundred pixels wide; a compressed version of the same photo, at the sharpness the eye actually sees, is several times lighter. Make it a habit before uploading any photo.

I bought cheap hosting. Is it really the culprit?

Sometimes yes and sometimes no. First check the photos and plugins, which are in your own hands. If those are fine and the site is still slow at busy hours, the hosting cannot answer for your shop, and changing it is more effective than any other optimization.

Should I fix speed first or the site’s look first?

Speed first. The customer has to see the page before its look can do anything. The good news is that lightening a site is usually cheaper and faster than a redesign, and after it, any design works better on a fast site.
